When exactly do I get the deposit back?

I have worked on a hotel front desk for nine years, and there are three lines on the booking page that nobody reads. The first one is the deposit. Almost every hotel takes a deposit when you book, and the money is not a payment, it is a hold. You get it back, but you get it back in ten working days, not on the day you leave. The second line is the fee for changing the date. Guests always tell me they cancelled, so they should get everything back. That is only true on a flexible rate. On the cheap rate, the room is non-refundable, and the word non-refundable means what it says. The third line is the one that costs people the most money, and it is the check-in time. If you land at six in the morning, your room is not ready at six. You are allowed to leave your bags with us free of charge, and most people do not know that.

Here is the question we get every week on this programme. Should you book the cheap rate or the flexible one? Look at the difference in price first. If the flexible rate costs fifteen per cent more, you are buying insurance, and the question is simply whether the trip is likely to change. A family holiday booked eleven months in advance is not the same as a work trip next Tuesday. The second thing to check is what the word refund actually means on that page. Some companies give you money; a lot of them give you a voucher, and a voucher is not a refund. And the third thing, which almost nobody does: save the confirmation e-mail as a file, not as an e-mail. If you have to argue at a desk in another country, the proof you can show on a screen in five seconds is worth more than the proof you have to look for.
